Problem 14 points
Ch. 1 — Scientific and Engineering Notation
A small-signal circuit draws a current of $0.000\,25\ \text{A}$. Express this current in scientific notation, then in engineering notation (power of ten a multiple of 3), and name the metric prefix that matches the engineering form.
Write $0.000\,25\ \text{A}$ in scientific notation and in engineering notation, and give the equivalent value with a metric prefix.[4 pts]
Answer: $2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A} = 250 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{A} = 250\ \mu\text{A}$ A
check: 0.00025 = 0.00025 ✗ (answer 250)
Worked Solution
Given: $I = 0.000\,25\ \text{A}$. Scientific notation: move the decimal point right until one nonzero digit is to its left. It moves 4 places, so $I = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A}$. Engineering notation: the exponent must be a multiple of 3. Moving the decimal 2 more places right gives 250 and lowers the exponent by 2: $I = 250 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{A}$. Since $10^{-6}$ is micro ($\mu$): $$I = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{A} = 250 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{A} = 250\ \mu\text{A}$$
Scientific notation keeps one digit before the decimal point. Engineering notation restricts exponents to multiples of 3 so they map directly onto metric prefixes.
Problem 26 points
Ch. 1 — Metric-Prefix Conversion
A capacitor in a parts bin is marked $47\,000\ \text{pF}$. Your schematic lists capacitor values in microfarads. Convert the marked value to microfarads, showing the prefix powers of ten you use.
Convert $47\,000\ \text{pF}$ to $\mu\text{F}$.[6 pts]
Answer: 0.047 µF
check: 47000e-12/1e-6 = 0.047 ✓
Worked Solution
Given: $C = 47\,000\ \text{pF}$. Prefix values: pico $= 10^{-12}$ and micro $= 10^{-6}$. Convert to base units: $C = 47\,000 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F} = 4.7 \times 10^{4} \times 10^{-12}\ \text{F} = 4.7 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{F}$. Convert to microfarads by dividing by $10^{-6}$: $$C = \frac{4.7 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{F}}{10^{-6}\ \text{F}/\mu\text{F}} = 4.7 \times 10^{-2}\ \mu\text{F} = 0.047\ \mu\text{F}$$ Check: micro is $10^{6}$ times larger than pico, so the number must shrink by $10^{6}$. $47\,000 / 10^{6} = 0.047$.
When converting to a larger prefix, the numeric value gets smaller by the ratio of the prefixes. From pico to micro, that ratio is $10^{6}$.
Problem 310 points
Ch. 1 — Significant Figures in Multi-Step Calculations
Three branch currents are measured as $12.45\ \text{mA}$, $3.1\ \text{mA}$, and $0.087\ \text{mA}$. They combine into one wire, and the total current flows for $12.0\ \text{s}$. The charge that passes is $Q = I t$. Find $Q$ in coulombs and report it with the correct number of significant figures. Carry unrounded intermediate values and round only at the end. State which measurement limits each step.
Find the total current, then the charge $Q$ in coulombs, reported to the correct significant figures.[10 pts]
Answer: 0.188 C
check: (12.45+3.1+0.087)*12.0/1000 = 0.187644 ✓
Worked Solution
Given: $I_1 = 12.45\ \text{mA}$, $I_2 = 3.1\ \text{mA}$, $I_3 = 0.087\ \text{mA}$, $t = 12.0\ \text{s}$. Step 1 (addition, where the least precise decimal place governs): $I = 12.45 + 3.1 + 0.087 = 15.637\ \text{mA}$. The value $3.1\ \text{mA}$ is known only to the tenths place, so the sum is good to $15.6\ \text{mA}$ (3 significant figures). Keep 15.637 as a guard value. Step 2 (multiplication, where the fewest significant figures govern): $Q = I t = (15.637 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A})(12.0\ \text{s}) = 0.187\,644\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$. Units: $\text{A}\cdot\text{s} = \text{C}$. Both factors carry 3 significant figures, so the result keeps 3: $$Q = 0.188\ \text{C} = 188\ \text{mC}$$ Note: rounding early to $15.6\ \text{mA}$ would give $15.6 \times 12.0 = 187.2\ \text{mC} \rightarrow 0.187\ \text{C}$. The last digit shifts, which is why you round only at the end.
Addition is limited by the least precise decimal place, and multiplication by the fewest significant figures. Carrying guard digits keeps rounding error from building up.
Problem 45 points
Ch. 1 — Unit Conversion
A rechargeable battery is rated at $2\,500\ \text{mAh}$ (milliampere-hours). Since $1\ \text{C} = 1\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$ and $1\ \text{h} = 3\,600\ \text{s}$, convert this rating to coulombs.
Express the $2\,500\ \text{mAh}$ rating as charge in coulombs.[5 pts]
Answer: 9000 C
check: 2500e-3*3600 = 9000 ✓
Worked Solution
Given: capacity $= 2\,500\ \text{mAh}$. Convert milliamperes to amperes: $2\,500\ \text{mA} = 2\,500 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 2.5\ \text{A}$, so the rating is $2.5\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h}$. Convert hours to seconds: $$Q = 2.5\ \text{A}\cdot\text{h} \times \frac{3\,600\ \text{s}}{1\ \text{h}} = 9\,000\ \text{A}\cdot\text{s}$$ Since $\text{A}\cdot\text{s} = \text{C}$: $Q = 9.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{C} = 9.0\ \text{kC}$.
A conversion factor equal to 1, such as $3\,600\ \text{s}/1\ \text{h}$, cancels the unwanted unit. Current multiplied by time is charge.
Problem 57 points
Ch. 1 — Reported Precision and Uncertainty
A digital multimeter displays $4.7163\ \text{V}$ across a component. The manufacturer's accuracy specification for this range is $\pm 0.5\%$ of the reading. Compute the uncertainty of the measurement. Round the uncertainty to one significant figure, then report the voltage in the form value $\pm$ uncertainty, keeping only the digits the uncertainty justifies.
Report the measured voltage with an appropriate number of digits, in the form $V \pm \Delta V$.[7 pts]
Answer: 4.72 ± 0.02 V
check: 4.7163 = 4.7163 ✗ (answer 0.02)
Worked Solution
Given: reading $V = 4.7163\ \text{V}$ and accuracy $\pm 0.5\%$ of reading. Uncertainty: $$\Delta V = 0.005 \times 4.7163\ \text{V} = 0.023\,58\ \text{V}$$ Rounded to one significant figure: $\Delta V \approx 0.02\ \text{V}$. The uncertainty is in the hundredths place, so digits past the hundredths place carry no information. Round the reading to the hundredths: $4.7163 \rightarrow 4.72\ \text{V}$. Reported result: $$V = 4.72 \pm 0.02\ \text{V}$$ The display shows five digits, but only three are meaningful.
A reading is only as precise as its uncertainty allows. Digits beyond the uncertainty's decimal place are noise, even if the display shows them.
Problem 610 points
Ch. 1 — Calculations in Powers of Ten
Without converting to ordinary decimals, evaluate $$X = \frac{(6.80 \times 10^{-3})(4.50 \times 10^{5})}{(1.50 \times 10^{-4})^{2}}$$ Handle the coefficients and the powers of ten separately. Give the result in scientific notation and in engineering notation, and name the metric prefix that matches the engineering form. Report 3 significant figures.
Evaluate $X$ in scientific and engineering notation, and name the matching metric prefix.[10 pts]
Answer: $1.36 \times 10^{11} = 136 \times 10^{9}$ (giga)
check: (6.80e-3*4.50e5)/(1.50e-4)^2 = 136000000000.00002 ✗ (answer 9)
Worked Solution
Numerator: multiply the coefficients and add the exponents. $(6.80)(4.50) = 30.6$ and $10^{-3} \times 10^{5} = 10^{2}$, so the numerator is $30.6 \times 10^{2} = 3.06 \times 10^{3}$. Denominator: square the coefficient and double the exponent. $(1.50)^2 = 2.25$ and $(10^{-4})^2 = 10^{-8}$, so the denominator is $2.25 \times 10^{-8}$. Divide: divide the coefficients and subtract the exponents. $$X = \frac{3.06}{2.25} \times 10^{3-(-8)} = 1.36 \times 10^{11}$$ Engineering notation: $1.36 \times 10^{11} = 136 \times 10^{9}$. The prefix for $10^{9}$ is giga (G), so $X = 136\ \text{G}$. All inputs have 3 significant figures, so the result keeps 3.
Powers of ten follow the exponent rules: add for products, subtract for quotients, multiply by $n$ for a power $n$. The coefficients are handled with ordinary arithmetic.
Problem 75 points
Ch. 2 — Current as Rate of Charge
During a test, $0.75\ \text{C}$ of charge passes a point in a wire in $250\ \text{ms}$. Using $I = Q/t$, find the current in amperes, and state in words what that value of current means.
Find the current $I$ and interpret its meaning.[5 pts]
Answer: 3.0 A
check: 0.75/0.250 = 3 ✓
Worked Solution
Given: $Q = 0.75\ \text{C}$ and $t = 250\ \text{ms} = 0.250\ \text{s}$. Current is the rate of charge flow: $$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{0.75\ \text{C}}{0.250\ \text{s}} = 3.0\ \text{C/s} = 3.0\ \text{A}$$ Interpretation: $3.0\ \text{A}$ means that 3.0 coulombs of charge pass the point every second. That is about $3.0 \times 6.25 \times 10^{18} = 1.9 \times 10^{19}$ electrons per second.
One ampere is one coulomb per second. Convert milliseconds to seconds before dividing.
Problem 87 points
Ch. 2 — Resistor Color Code and Tolerance
A 4-band resistor has the bands yellow, violet, red, gold, read from left to right. The color code is: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. A gold fourth band means $\pm 5\%$ tolerance. Decode the nominal resistance and tolerance. Then find the minimum and maximum resistance the part can have and still be in tolerance. Give the maximum as your final answer.
Decode the resistor, find its tolerance range, and give the maximum in-tolerance resistance in kilohms.[7 pts]
Answer: 4.935 kΩ
check: 4700*1.05/1000 = 4.935 ✓
Worked Solution
Band 1 (yellow) $= 4$ and band 2 (violet) $= 7$, so the first two digits are 47. Band 3 (red) is the multiplier $10^{2}$. Nominal: $R = 47 \times 10^{2}\ \Omega = 4\,700\ \Omega = 4.7\ \text{k}\Omega$. Band 4 (gold) gives $\pm 5\%$ tolerance. Tolerance amount: $\Delta R = 0.05 \times 4\,700\ \Omega = 235\ \Omega$. Range: $$R_{\min} = 4\,700 - 235 = 4\,465\ \Omega = 4.465\ \text{k}\Omega$$ $$R_{\max} = 4\,700 + 235 = 4\,935\ \Omega = 4.935\ \text{k}\Omega$$
The first two bands are digits, the third is a power-of-ten multiplier, and the fourth sets the percentage band around the nominal value.
Problem 910 points
Ch. 2 — DMM Range, Resolution, and Accuracy
A manual-ranging $3\tfrac{1}{2}$-digit DMM (maximum display 1999 counts) has DC voltage ranges of 200 mV, 2 V, 20 V, 200 V, and 1000 V. It is used to measure a supply whose true voltage is $18.736\ \text{V}$. Determine what the display shows on the 2 V, 20 V, and 200 V ranges, and choose the range that gives the best resolution. On that range, the accuracy specification is $\pm(0.5\%\ \text{of reading} + 2\ \text{counts})$. Compute the worst-case uncertainty of the reading on the best range.
DMM DC voltage ranges (3½-digit, 1999 counts)
Range     Max display   Resolution (1 count)
200 mV    199.9 mV      0.1 mV
2 V       1.999 V       0.001 V
20 V      19.99 V       0.01 V
200 V     199.9 V       0.1 V
1000 V    1000 V        1 V
Find the displays on the 2 V, 20 V, and 200 V ranges, choose the best range, and compute the worst-case uncertainty on that range.[10 pts]
Answer: 0.114 V
check: 0.005*18.74+2*0.01 = 0.1137 ✓
Worked Solution
2 V range: its maximum display is $1.999\ \text{V}$, and $18.736\ \text{V}$ exceeds that, so the display shows OL (overload). 20 V range: the resolution is $0.01\ \text{V}$, so the display shows $18.74\ \text{V}$. 200 V range: the resolution is $0.1\ \text{V}$, so the display shows $18.7\ \text{V}$. The best range is the lowest one that does not overload: the 20 V range, with four displayed digits. Uncertainty on the 20 V range, where one count is $0.01\ \text{V}$: $$\Delta V = 0.005 \times 18.74\ \text{V} + 2 \times 0.01\ \text{V} = 0.0937 + 0.020 = 0.1137\ \text{V}$$ So $\Delta V \approx 0.114\ \text{V}$, or about $\pm 0.11\ \text{V}$. The true value lies between about $18.63\ \text{V}$ and $18.85\ \text{V}$.
The lowest range that does not overload gives the finest resolution. A count-based accuracy specification adds a fixed number of least-significant digits to the percentage error.
Problem 105 points
Ch. 2 — Setting Up a Current Measurement
A series circuit consists of a $9\ \text{V}$ battery, a switch S1, and a resistor R1. Point A is the junction between S1 and R1, and point B is the junction between R1 and the battery's negative terminal. You must measure the current through R1 with a digital multimeter. List, in order, how you prepare the meter and connect it to the circuit. State the one connection you must never make with the meter in current mode.
Series circuit for the current measurement
Describe the meter setup and the connection procedure for measuring the current through R1.[5 pts]
Answer: (1) Open S1 to remove power. (2) Set the DMM to DC current (A or mA) on a range higher than the expected current. (3) Move the red lead to the A/mA jack and leave the black lead in COM. (4) Break the circuit at point A and insert the meter in series, with current entering the red lead and leaving the black lead. (5) Close S1 and read the current, stepping down the range if needed. (6) Remove power before disconnecting. Never place the meter in current mode across (in parallel with) R1 or the battery. Its very low internal resistance creates a near short circuit that can blow the fuse or damage the meter.
Worked Solution
An ammeter must carry the same current as R1, so it must be in series with R1. Procedure: (1) Open S1 so no current flows while you rewire. (2) Select DC current on the DMM, starting on a range above the expected value. (3) Move the red test lead to the A or mA jack and keep the black lead in COM. (4) Open the circuit at point A and connect the meter across the gap, with the red lead toward S1 (the positive side) and the black lead toward R1. The meter then completes the loop. (5) Close S1 and read the current, moving to a lower range if the reading is small. (6) Open S1 again, remove the meter, reconnect the circuit, and return the red lead to the V/Ω jack. The connection you must never make: the meter in current mode placed in parallel with R1 or the battery. An ammeter has very low resistance, so this shorts the source and can blow the fuse or damage the meter.
Ammeters go in series and voltmeters go in parallel. Because an ammeter has very low resistance, placing it in parallel creates a short circuit.
Problem 117 points
Ch. 2 — Meter Safety Reasoning
After a current measurement, a student leaves the red lead in the meter's 10 A jack with the function switch still on DC amps. The student then touches the probes across a $12.0\ \text{V}$ lead-acid battery, intending to measure its voltage. The total resistance of the path (meter shunt, fuse, leads, and battery internal resistance) is $0.050\ \Omega$. Using $I = V/R$, estimate the current that would flow. Compare it with the meter's $10\ \text{A}$ fuse rating, explain the hazards, and state what the student should have done.
Estimate the current, compare it with the fuse rating, and explain the hazard and the correct procedure.[7 pts]
Answer: 240 A
check: 12.0/0.050 = 240 ✓
Worked Solution
Given: $V = 12.0\ \text{V}$ and $R = 0.050\ \Omega$. Estimated current: $$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12.0\ \text{V}}{0.050\ \Omega} = 240\ \text{A}$$ Ratio to the fuse rating: $240/10 = 24$, so the current is 24 times what the fuse is rated for. Hazards: an ammeter is a near short circuit. A lead-acid battery can deliver very large currents, so the fuse blows. If the fuse is under-rated or missing, the leads and meter can overheat, arc, or melt, and the battery can vent hydrogen, risking burns or an explosion. Correct procedure: before measuring voltage, move the red lead back to the V/Ω jack, set the function switch to DC volts, and only then place the probes in parallel across the battery. Always check the jack and function settings before touching probes to a source.
A meter in current mode has almost no resistance. Connecting it across a voltage source creates a short circuit, and the current is limited only by very small resistances.
Problem 1210 points
Ch. 2 — Energy, Charge, Current, and Electrons
A $9.0\ \text{V}$ battery delivers $540\ \text{J}$ of energy to a circuit over $2.0\ \text{min}$. Use $V = W/Q$, $I = Q/t$, and the constant $1\ \text{C} \approx 6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons. Find the charge moved, the average current, and the number of electrons that passed through the battery. Give the number of electrons as your final answer.
Find $Q$, $I$, and the number of electrons. The number of electrons is the final answer.[10 pts]
Answer: $3.75 \times 10^{20}$ electrons
check: (540/9.0)*6.25e18 = 375000000000000000000 ✗ (answer 20)
Worked Solution
Given: $V = 9.0\ \text{V}$, $W = 540\ \text{J}$, $t = 2.0\ \text{min} = 120\ \text{s}$. Charge, rearranging $V = W/Q$: $$Q = \frac{W}{V} = \frac{540\ \text{J}}{9.0\ \text{J/C}} = 60\ \text{C}$$ Average current: $$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{60\ \text{C}}{120\ \text{s}} = 0.50\ \text{A}$$ Number of electrons: $$n = 60\ \text{C} \times 6.25 \times 10^{18}\ \frac{\text{electrons}}{\text{C}} = 375 \times 10^{18} = 3.75 \times 10^{20}\ \text{electrons}$$ Units check: $\text{J} / (\text{J/C}) = \text{C}$ and $\text{C}/\text{s} = \text{A}$.
Voltage is energy per unit charge, current is charge per unit time, and one coulomb is about $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.
Problem 137 points
Integrated — Interpreting Logged Current Data
A data logger recorded the current drawn by a sensor module at five evenly spaced times during a $5.0\ \text{min}$ test. The readings are shown in the exhibit, in milliamperes. Find the average current, then use $Q = I t$ to find the total charge delivered during the test, in coulombs. Show all unit conversions.
Logged current readings
Sample   Time (min)   Current (mA)
1        0.0          120
2        1.25         118
3        2.50         122
4        3.75         121
5        5.00         119
Compute the average current and the total charge delivered over the $5.0\ \text{min}$ test.[7 pts]
Answer: 36 C
check: (120+118+122+121+119)/5/1000*5.0*60 = 36 ✓
Worked Solution
Average current: $$I_{avg} = \frac{120 + 118 + 122 + 121 + 119}{5}\ \text{mA} = \frac{600}{5}\ \text{mA} = 120\ \text{mA}$$ Conversions: $I_{avg} = 120 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 0.120\ \text{A}$ and $t = 5.0\ \text{min} \times 60\ \text{s/min} = 300\ \text{s}$. Charge: $$Q = I_{avg}\, t = (0.120\ \text{A})(300\ \text{s}) = 36\ \text{C}$$ Since $t$ is given to 2 significant figures, $Q = 36\ \text{C}$.
Converting data to base SI units before combining them keeps the result in coulombs. Averaging nearly constant readings gives a representative current.
Problem 147 points
Integrated — Combining Quantities with Different Prefixes
Three currents flow into a node: $I_1 = 1.2\ \text{mA}$, $I_2 = 350\ \mu\text{A}$, and $I_3 = 0.000\,45\ \text{A}$. The total current leaving the node is their sum. Convert all three to milliamperes, add them, and report the total in milliamperes with correct precision. Also express the total in microamperes using engineering notation.
Find the total current in milliamperes, and restate it in microamperes.[7 pts]
Answer: 2.0 mA
check: (1.2e-3+350e-6+0.00045)*1000 = 2 ✓
Worked Solution
Convert each current to milliamperes. $I_1 = 1.2\ \text{mA}$. $I_2 = 350\ \mu\text{A} = 350 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{A} = 0.350\ \text{mA}$. $I_3 = 0.000\,45\ \text{A} = 0.45 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 0.45\ \text{mA}$. Sum: $$I_T = 1.2 + 0.350 + 0.45 = 2.00\ \text{mA}$$ Precision: $1.2\ \text{mA}$ is known only to the tenths place, so $I_T = 2.0\ \text{mA}$. In microamperes: $I_T = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 2.0 \times 10^{3}\ \mu\text{A}$ (about $2\,000\ \mu\text{A}$).
Quantities must share the same prefix before they can be added. The least precise term sets the precision of the sum.
